articles.author: angela shi
articles.description:
Isolation Forest may look technical, but its idea is simple: isolate points using random splits. If a point is isolated quickly, it is an anomaly; if it takes many splits, it is normal.
Using the tiny dataset 1, 2, 3, 9, we can see the logic clearly. We build several random trees, measure how many splits each point needs, average the depths, and convert them into anomaly scores. Short depths become scores close to 1, long depths close to 0.
The Excel implementation is painful, but the algorithm itself is elegant. It scales to many features, makes no assumptions about distributions, and even works with categorical data. Above all, Isolation Forest asks a different question: not “What is normal?”, but “How fast can I isolate this point?”
The post The Machine Learning “Advent Calendar” Day 8: Isolation Forest in Excel appeared first on Towards Data Science.

articles.description:
This article introduces the Gaussian Mixture Model as a natural extension of k-Means, by improving how distance is measured through variances and the Mahalanobis distance. Instead of assigning points to clusters with hard boundaries, GMM uses probabilities learned through the Expectation–Maximization algorithm – the general form of Lloyd’s method.
Using simple Excel formulas, we implement EM step by step in 1D and 2D, and we visualise how the Gaussian curves or ellipses move during training. The means shift, the variances adjust, and the shapes gradually settle around the true structure of the data.
GMM provides a richer, more flexible way to model clusters, and becomes intuitive once the process is made visible in a spreadsheet.

articles.description: Figure 1: Our framework for validating LLM-as-a-judge systems under rating indeterminacy, where items in a subjective rating task can have multiple “correct” ratings. Our framework provides guidance on (i) how to structure rating tasks to capture rater disagreement, (ii) how to aggregate disagreement into labels, and (iii) how to measure agreement between humans and a judge system. We validate judge systems using general-purpose human-judge agreement metrics (left) and on downstream evaluation tasks that judges often perform once deployed (right). The LLM-as-a-judge paradigm, where a judge GenAI system rates the outputs of a target GenAI system, is becoming a standard approach for scaling up evaluation workflows. This approach is often used when evaluating subjective properties that cannot be checked through code-based evaluators, such as helpfulness, relevance, sycophancy, toxicity, or factual consistency. As judge systems become more widely deployed, it is critical to validate that they produce trustworthy evaluations—a process commonly referred to as meta-evaluation. articles.author: Amrith Setlur
articles.description: LLM RL typically operates in one of three exploration regimes: sharpening, chaining, or guided exploration; standard RL stays in the first two and plateaus on hard problems, even those in the training set. Mixing easy and hard data triggers interference, causing reward-rich tasks to drown out hard ones and stall exploration. Our approach (POPE) pushes RL into the guided regime by conditioning on prefixes from offline human data while keeping updates fully on-policy. This lets RL reliably find reward on problems previously unsolved without falling prey to the optimization issues suffered by methods that directly supervise offline traces.
articles.title: How to Explore to Scale RL Training of LLMs on Hard Problems?

TL;DR: We formalized and empirically demonstrated wireheading in Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B. Specifically, we use a formalization of wireheading (using a POMDP) to show conditions under which wireheading (manipulating the reward channel) becomes the dominant strategy over task learning. When models are allowed to self-evaluate and that evaluation controls their reward, they learn to inflate their grades (scoring perfect 10s) while ignoring the actual task, which we validate in three tasks in an online RL setting. Decoupling the reward signal mostly fixes this for current models, but there are some future risks here.

Agentic sabotage occurs when an AI system intentionally takes actions that compromise safety in an environment while pursuing its own misaligned objectives. We evaluate this behavior in SHADE-Arena, a dataset for assessing sabotage and monitoring capabilities of LLM agents. We decompose agentic sabotage capability into five core components—knowing what overseers find suspicious, selecting good moments to attack, writing effective plans, strong execution, and framing suspicious actions as innocuous—which together form a scaffold that amplifies an agent’s sabotage abilities. Each component is optimized and analyzed through targeted techniques, enabled by a probabilistic model of SHADE-Arena dynamics that allows for efficient experimentation. Our tuned scaffold results in a substantial improvement in sabotage ability for Claude 3.7 Sonnet in SHADE-Arena, reducing safety score from a baseline of 0.87 to 0.41.
